passage: Thomas, you asked why the family calls me Sarita the Sword. At fifteen I said everything straight. I told my best friend her poem was too long, in front of the whole class, and she cried in the washroom. I'm not proud of that one. But that same year, when the girls in my class decided to freeze out the new girl from the hostel, everyone went along. I didn't. I sat with her every lunch and told the ringleader to her face that it was cruel. I didn't need them to like me. I lost two friends and gained one for life. Your Ammachi still says hard things, mon. I've just learned to say them a little kinder.

qa.q: What did Sarita tell her best friend about her poem?
qa.a: She told her best friend her poem was too long, in front of the whole class.

qa.q: How does Sarita feel now about the poem comment?
qa.a: She is not proud of it; she sees that her bluntness hurt her friend.

qa.q: What choice did young Sarita make when the class froze out the new girl?
qa.a: She refused to go along, sat with the new girl every lunch and told the ringleader it was cruel.

qa.q: How might the new girl have experienced Sarita sitting with her every lunch?
qa.a: She probably felt less alone and protected, which may be why they became friends for life.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being a blunt teenager whose words once hurt a friend but whose independence let her stand up against unfair exclusion.

passage: Forty minutes before the science project was due, with the school printer jammed and the group crowded round one laptop, Sarita scrolled to Nilesh's section and stopped. "This is copied. Word for word." Nilesh's face fell. "We don't have time, Sarita." "Then we submit less, not stolen." The others groaned; one called her a teacher's pet. She didn't care. She rewrote the key paragraph herself, fast and plain, while they fixed the printer. They submitted with three minutes left. On the stairs she saw Nilesh walking alone and remembered how she'd said it, loudly, in front of everyone. She caught up. "I shouldn't have announced it. Your diagrams were the best part." He gave a half-smile.

qa.q: How long before the deadline did Sarita spot the copied section?
qa.a: Forty minutes before the science project was due.

qa.q: Why did Sarita catch up with Nilesh on the stairs?
qa.a: She realised her loud announcement had hurt him and wanted to make it right.

qa.q: Which choice under time pressure showed Sarita's strength?
qa.a: She refused to submit copied work and rewrote the paragraph herself, holding firm even when called a teacher's pet.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when Sarita called out the copying in front of everyone?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and hurt; his face fell, and afterwards he walked alone.

grounding: Under deadline pressure a teenager bluntly refuses copied work despite being mocked, then notices her tone hurt a classmate.

passage:
'So? Did you like my poem?'
'Honestly? The first half, yes. The ending's a greeting card.'
Gurpreet's face fell. 'Wow. Thanks, Ayesha.'
'You asked.'
'I asked if you liked it, not for a post-mortem.'
Ayesha opened her mouth, then shut it. 'Okay. That came out harsh. The first half really is good.'
That evening someone posted the class trip list in the group chat. Meher, the new girl, had been left off. 'She's weird,' someone wrote. Six laughing replies.
Ayesha typed: 'Put her back on. That's not fair and you know it.'
Silence. Then Gurpreet, still annoyed, messaged her privately: 'You're impossible. But you're right.'

qa.q: What did Ayesha say about the poem's ending?
qa.a: That it's a greeting card.

qa.q: What does Ayesha opening her mouth and then shutting it suggest?
qa.a: She realised she had hurt Gurpreet and felt a flicker of regret before softening her words.

qa.q: What could Ayesha keep, and what could she change, about her honesty?
qa.a: Keep speaking up against unfairness, as with the trip list; change the delivery of feedback by leading with what works.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Ayesha by the end of the day?
qa.a: Gurpreet is still stung about the poem but respects that Ayesha stood up for Meher: 'You're impossible. But you're right.'

grounding: Shows a teenager whose bluntness hurts a friend, and whose same honesty resists the group and speaks up against unfairness.

passage: In Class 11 I lost two friends in one week, and I'd do half of it again. I'm Dolma. I run the 800 metres, and I've never pretended I don't want to win. When Aparna beat me at districts, I told her straight: 'You ran smarter. I'm coming for you next time.' She laughed; we're still close. But then Coach picked the relay team from the ones who'd stayed back to help at his daughter's birthday, not the fastest. Everyone grumbled in the changing room. Only I said it to his face, calmly, with the timings on paper. Two teammates stopped talking to me; they said I'd made them look bad. Coach redid the trials. Maybe I could have said it in private first. That part I'd change. The rest, no.

qa.q: What did Dolma bring when speaking to Coach?
qa.a: The timings on paper.

qa.q: How does Dolma feel, looking back at that week?
qa.a: Dolma feels mostly sure speaking up was right, with a little regret about how and where it was said.

qa.q: What would Dolma change about raising the relay issue?
qa.a: Saying it to Coach in private first, while still using the timings to make a calm, fair case.

qa.q: Why might the two teammates have stopped talking to Dolma?
qa.a: They felt embarrassed and exposed, as if Dolma's challenge showed them going along with something unfair.

grounding: Shows a teenager who competes openly, doesn't need everyone's approval, and speaks up against an unfair selection at a cost to some friendships.

passage:
Class 10B, notes after the parent meeting: Vidya
Vidya is one of the most honest students I teach. In Tuesday's debate practice she told Karan, 'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.' She was not wrong, but he went red and didn't speak again. Afterwards I talked with her about saying the hard thing without the sting. She listened, arms folded, then said, 'Fine. But I won't pretend it was good.' Fair enough. The same week, when most of the class agreed to share answers for the online quiz, Vidya refused and told them why, in front of everyone. Nobody else did. Her parents worry she has no friends. I see a student who doesn't need permission to be fair. We agreed she'll start her feedback with one thing that works.
Ujjwal, class teacher

qa.q: What did Vidya say to Karan in debate practice?
qa.a: 'That argument is lazy. You didn't read the article.'

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt refusing to share quiz answers in front of everyone?
qa.a: She probably felt firm and determined, maybe uncomfortable, but not needing the class's approval to do what was fair.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal and Vidya agree, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: That she will start feedback with one thing that works; it keeps her honesty but lessens the sting for classmates like Karan.

qa.q: How might Karan have felt after Vidya's comment?
qa.a: Karan felt embarrassed, going red and staying silent for the rest of the practice.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a teenager whose blunt honesty can hurt but who also resists peer pressure and refuses to join in cheating.

passage:
Wednesday
Told Mawii her song for the school contest was off-key in the second verse. It WAS. But she went quiet and walked off, and I felt bad all through maths. I always say the hard thing. Sometimes I should say it softer.
But then at lunch, the girls started laughing at the new girl's accent, and they looked at me to join in. I didn't. I said, "That's not funny." Nobody spoke to me for the rest of lunch. I don't care. Well, I care a bit.
And in PE I told Francis Sir straight out that picking the team captain by who's tallest isn't fair. He actually listened and said we'd vote next week.
Tonight I'll text Mawii sorry for how I said it. Not for what I said.
Lalremsiami

qa.q: What did Francis Sir agree to do next week?
qa.a: Let the class vote for the team captain.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after telling Mawii her song was off-key?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt bad all through maths, knowing the honest words hurt Mawii.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami's bluntness help in other moments?
qa.a: It lets Lalremsiami refuse to join the mocking and speak up about the unfair captain rule.

qa.q: How might Mawii feel after getting the apology text?
qa.a: Mawii may feel hurt still but soothed, understanding the feedback was honest, not cruel.

grounding: Shows a blunt teenager whose honesty can hurt a friend but who resists peer pressure and speaks up against unfairness, learning to soften the tone.
